text: The worker_connections directive sets the maximum number of simultaneous connections a single Nginx worker process can handle. If your server hits connection limits under load, raising worker_connections in the events block along with the OS file descriptor limit usually resolves it.

A 502 Bad Gateway error in Nginx usually means the upstream application server closed the connection, crashed, or timed out before sending a response. Check the upstream service logs first, then verify proxy_pass points to a reachable address.

A 504 Gateway Timeout happens when Nginx waits longer than proxy_read_timeout for the backend to respond. Increasing proxy_read_timeout and proxy_connect_timeout can help for slow backend operations, but the root cause is usually a slow upstream process.

To apply configuration changes without dropping active connections, run 'nginx -s reload'. This makes Nginx re-read nginx.conf, start new worker processes with the updated config, and gracefully shut down the old workers.

Before reloading, always validate the configuration with 'nginx -t'. This checks the syntax of nginx.conf and all included files and reports the exact line number of any error, preventing a bad reload from taking the server down.

The server_name directive defines which domain names a particular server block responds to. Nginx matches incoming requests against server_name values to decide which block should handle the request, supporting exact names, wildcards, and regular expressions.

The listen directive specifies the IP address and port a server block listens on, such as 'listen 80;' or 'listen 443 ssl;'. Multiple listen directives can be combined with server_name to host several sites on one machine.

To configure Nginx as a reverse proxy, use 'proxy_pass http://backend_address;' inside a location block. Nginx forwards incoming client requests to the specified backend and returns the backend's response to the client.
Nginx's default load balancing method distributes requests across servers listed in an upstream block in simple round-robin order, sending each new request to the next server in the list.
The least_conn load balancing method sends new requests to the backend server with the fewest currently active connections, which helps when backend requests take variable amounts of time to process.

The ssl_certificate and ssl_certificate_key directives point Nginx to the public certificate file and private key used for HTTPS. Both must be present and correctly referenced inside a server block listening on an SSL-enabled port.

An SSL handshake failure often occurs because of an expired certificate, a mismatched certificate chain, or an unsupported cipher between client and server. Checking certificate expiry and the ssl_protocols directive is the first troubleshooting step.
A common way to force HTTPS is a server block listening on port 80 that returns a permanent redirect, using 'return 301 https://$host$request_uri;' inside the location block matching all paths.

Enabling 'gzip on;' along with 'gzip_types' compresses responses of specified MIME types before sending them to the client, reducing bandwidth usage and improving load times for text-based assets like CSS and JavaScript.

The client_max_body_size directive limits the maximum allowed size of a client request body. Uploads larger than this limit are rejected with a 413 Request Entity Too Large error, so file-upload endpoints often need this raised.

A 413 error means the incoming request body exceeded the limit set by client_max_body_size. Increasing this directive in the relevant server or location block, then reloading Nginx, resolves the error for legitimate large uploads.
The rewrite directive changes the requested URI based on a regular expression before it is processed further, commonly used for legacy URL redirection or cleaning up query parameters.

Nginx location blocks match request URIs using prefix strings, exact matches with '=', or regular expressions with '~' and '~*'. The most specific matching rule generally takes precedence when multiple location blocks could apply.

try_files checks for the existence of files in the given order and serves the first one found, commonly used to serve static files if present and fall back to an application server or index file otherwise.
error_page maps specific HTTP status codes to a custom URI or file, allowing administrators to show friendly custom error pages for codes like 404 or 500 instead of the default Nginx error output.

access_log records every request Nginx handles, including client IP, request line, and status code, while error_log records warnings and errors from the Nginx process itself, both essential for debugging.
The log_format directive lets administrators define custom fields for access_log entries, such as request time or upstream response time, which is useful when diagnosing performance issues.
limit_req_zone combined with limit_req implements request rate limiting per client IP, protecting backend services from being overwhelmed by too many requests in a short time window.
limit_conn_zone and limit_conn restrict the number of simultaneous connections allowed from a single client, which helps mitigate certain abuse patterns without blocking legitimate traffic entirely.
Setting 'worker_processes auto;' tells Nginx to automatically spawn one worker process per available CPU core, which is the recommended setting for most production deployments to maximize throughput.
keepalive_timeout controls how long an idle keep-alive connection between client and server stays open before Nginx closes it, balancing connection reuse against tying up worker resources.

proxy_set_header forwards additional headers to the upstream server when proxying, commonly used to pass the original Host, X-Real-IP, and X-Forwarded-For headers so the backend knows the true client details.

In the open-source version, Nginx marks an upstream server as temporarily unavailable after a configured number of failed attempts using max_fails and fail_timeout, routing traffic away from it until it recovers.

proxy_cache_path defines a cache storage location and proxy_cache enables caching of upstream responses in a location block, reducing repeated load on backend servers for frequently requested content.

The open-source Nginx build does not include built-in selective cache purging; administrators typically work around this by using cache keys that include query parameters or by clearing the cache directory manually.
The index directive specifies which file to serve when a request maps to a directory, such as 'index index.html index.htm;', with Nginx trying each filename in order until one is found.

The root directive appends the request URI to a base path, while alias replaces the matched location portion of the URI entirely, a distinction that frequently causes 404 errors when the two are confused.
A 404 from Nginx for a file that exists on disk is usually caused by an incorrect root or alias path, wrong file permissions, or a location block regex that does not match the intended URI.
A 403 Forbidden response commonly results from incorrect file or directory permissions, a missing index file with autoindex off, or explicit deny rules in the configuration blocking the client's IP.

Setting 'autoindex on;' inside a location block makes Nginx generate a simple directory listing page when no index file is present, useful for file-serving directories but usually disabled in production for security.
The allow and deny directives, evaluated in order, restrict access to a location based on client IP address or CIDR range, commonly used to protect admin endpoints or internal-only paths.
auth_basic combined with auth_basic_user_file enables HTTP basic authentication for a location, prompting clients for a username and password checked against an htpasswd-formatted credentials file.

The map directive creates a new variable whose value depends on the value of another variable, commonly used to conditionally set headers or redirect targets based on request attributes like User-Agent.
Nginx exposes built-in variables such as $request_uri, $host, $remote_addr, and $args that can be used throughout the configuration to build dynamic responses, logs, and proxy behavior.

The include directive pulls the contents of another file into the configuration at that point, commonly used to keep server blocks for different sites in separate files under sites-available and sites-enabled.
The common Debian/Ubuntu convention stores full site configurations in sites-available and symlinks the active ones into sites-enabled, which is then included from the main nginx.conf.

worker_rlimit_nofile raises the maximum number of open file descriptors a worker process may use, which needs to be increased alongside worker_connections when scaling to handle many concurrent connections.

Enabling HTTP/2 by adding 'http2 on;' (or the older 'listen 443 ssl http2;' syntax) allows Nginx to multiplex multiple requests over a single connection, reducing latency for clients loading many assets.
The stub_status module, enabled with 'stub_status;' in a location block, exposes basic real-time metrics like active connections and total requests handled, useful for monitoring dashboards.
A full restart of Nginx drops all active connections and briefly stops serving traffic, while a reload via 'nginx -s reload' applies new configuration without interrupting in-flight requests.

An nginx.conf file is organized into contexts: the top-level main context, the events block, and one or more http blocks containing server blocks, each nested context inheriting settings from its parent unless overridden.

Adding 'default_server' to a listen directive designates that server block as the fallback for requests whose Host header does not match any other server_name, preventing unexpected routing to the first-defined block.

Setting a 'keepalive' value inside an upstream block allows Nginx to maintain a pool of persistent connections to backend servers, reducing the overhead of establishing new TCP connections for every proxied request.

proxy_buffering controls whether Nginx buffers the response from an upstream server before sending it to the client; disabling it can reduce latency for streaming responses but increases load on the backend.
The sendfile directive lets the OS transfer static file contents directly from disk to the network socket without copying through userspace, improving performance when serving large static files.
Restricting ssl_protocols to modern versions like TLSv1.2 and TLSv1.3, and disabling older protocols such as TLSv1.0 and TLSv1.1, is a standard hardening step to avoid known cryptographic weaknesses.

Adding the Strict-Transport-Security header via add_header instructs browsers to only connect to the site over HTTPS for a specified duration, helping prevent protocol downgrade and cookie-hijacking attacks.
Combining error_page with a location block serving a static HTML file lets a site show a branded error page for statuses like 500 or 502 instead of the plain default Nginx error text.
For pure static sites, a minimal server block with root pointing at the file directory and try_files falling back to index.html is enough for Nginx to serve all assets efficiently.

Proxying WebSocket connections through Nginx requires setting 'proxy_http_version 1.1;' along with Upgrade and Connection headers via proxy_set_header so the connection can be upgraded from HTTP to the WebSocket protocol.
worker_shutdown_timeout sets how long Nginx waits for a worker process to finish handling in-flight requests during a graceful shutdown before forcefully terminating it.
Nginx does not rotate logs on its own; log rotation is typically handled externally by logrotate, which renames the log file and sends Nginx a USR1 signal to reopen fresh log files.

By default Nginx worker processes do not inherit most environment variables from the shell; the env directive in the main context must explicitly list which variables should be passed through, such as for API keys used in Lua scripts.
A single server block can respond to several domains by listing them all in server_name separated by spaces, which is convenient when multiple hostnames should serve identical content.

Setting the error_log directive's level to 'debug' produces extremely verbose diagnostic output useful for tracing exactly how Nginx processes a request, though it is far too noisy to leave enabled in production.
